I'm here for the Travis Scott…” And he's like, “You got the wrong house, buddy.” I was at somebody else’s house.

So I start walking back to the gate, and the gate is not opening. So now I gotta walk back up the driveway, ring the dude's doorbell and be like, can you let me out? So I get it out and I'm trying to call some people from Travis’ team. Apparently there was a search party trying to find me. So I see in the distance five flashlights just moving around. I'm like, “Yo, I'm right here! I'm coming.” Malibu is the worst place at nighttime if you don't have a car, bro. It's insane. But that's not the worst story.

OK, boom. It's Travis, it's his video guy… It’s like a YouTube video. So Travis is super cool. He's playing his music. One of the first things that I played, I was trying to make sure that I played the weirdest thing that he would not expect to hop on. So I play him this weird Afrobeat type of beat that I called Afrofuturism. It's this crazy epic futuristic sound.

But then, he's like, “I think you should try to add something to the song I have with Bad Bunny.” And just like the Drake story, I look calm on the outside but on the inside, I’m running laps. So I play the song, and it’s crazy. He didn't even say The freaking Weeknd was on the song. But he sends me the files or whatever, and I start working on it.

But the next day was cool, because I got to Shangri-La at the same time Travis got to the gate. Travis pulls up in this chocolate Lamborghini Urus truck and he rolls down his window and is like, “Hop in.” Let me remind you, this is all new to me. It was a 42-second drive up the driveway, but it was the craziest 40 seconds ever. But this is crazy, too. So we go in—it's just me and Travis, and everyone's coming in later. We're just playing shit, just chopping it up, talking about this show called _Gangs of London_.

And then this director dude comes in who directed these crazy movies. I forget his name. During that conversation, this tall dude with this huge beard comes waltzing in with this vintage T-shirt and super old sneakers on. You know who it was? Bon Iver. Bro, no cap, I almost fainted. I was like, this day can not get any crazier.

Then Bon Iver was like, “I just built a studio in the middle of nowhere. Yung Lean came. You should come. it would be dope.” But as the day went on, WondaGurl came in, and I'm a huge WondaGurl fan. It was the first time that I met her in person. I was geeked. She's one of my G.O.A.T.s, man. Anyway, I worked on two songs, “K-Pop” and “Sirens.” Then it was time to leave Malibu.

In Malibu, the Uber system does not work after 9 p.m. So I had to schedule a car service to take me to the airport because my flight was at 6 a.m. So I just crashed at Shangri-La. I wake up, 2:50 a.m. I grab my bags. It's pitch black. I realized that I left my bag in the main studio. So I go to the main studio and it’s locked. But I’m like, I'm going to be back in Cali next week; I'll just grab it, because if I don't make this flight, my wife's gonna kill me.

So I got my suitcase, and I walk down this super long driveway. It's abnormally long. I get to the gate, I see the car guy, but the gate is not open. So I'm calling people, and no one's responding because it's 3 o'clock in the freaking morning. I run back with my suitcase, trying to find someone to let me out of this building. I was looking in every room. Rick Rubin was probably like, who is this guy at 3 a.m. going through my house like this?

So I'm looking through everything, but I don't see a button or clicker. The driver calls me and says his company policy is not to wait over 30 minutes. So I got 10 minutes to figure out how the hell I want to get out of this place. So I'm looking on the counter, and then under a pile of ketchup, I found a house phone, and on the back there's a number to open the garage. Thank God. So I start walking down, and by the time I got to the gate, the gate is closed. So I sprint up the driveway, then run back down the driveway. And made it.

But then the man was like, “I don't know if I can take you because \[it’s past 30 minutes\].” I'm like, “Bro, it's only been one minute.” He was going to call his boss and see if it's cool. He hops in his car, sits there for like a minute, and the dude drives away. He drives away! My jaw was on the floor.

**So how does this story end?**  
I call Ubers from 3:35 a.m. to about 6 a.m. in the morning. I was outside. It's cold. I had the Uber and the Lyft app back to back. Find a ride, no ride, find a ride, no ride. No drivers available. There’s no way Malibu is a real place. I felt like fucking Tom Hanks in that one movie where he was stranded.

**_Cast Away_?**  
Yeah! My suitcase was like his soccer ball. It felt so long. I was just pacing back and forth for almost two hours, bro. I'm parched; I can barely breathe. I swear I grew a beard or something.

**It's like, you have great circumstances and then also just terrible luck.**  
Oh, a whole lot of terrible luck. But anyway, “Meltdown” was made during the tour. Drake sets us up in New York, and I’m staying at the same hotel as Drake. And Drake had us wear these blue tracksuits that he made for Nike. So I would wear that, and there’s paparazzi outside. People would just automatically assume you were with his crew. So they just start taking mad pictures of me. I’m like, “I’m just trying to grab a bagel, bro.” It was crazy.

But anyway, he sets up a studio; we start working. This is a Tuesday, and _Utopia_ comes out Friday. So Drake is like, “I like the song where it's at so far, but I feel like Travis' part, it could be even bigger.” Because Drake and Travis rapped on the same beat. So he was like, “Yo, Benny, can you make a transition, and then make Travis' part bigger? I'm gonna send you the files.”

Mind you, I didn’t know Drake rapped on the beat for _Utopia_. I was in Cali watching _Cocomelon_ on super dad mode. I’m like holy shit. So I get to work, put my headphones on. My kids are running around. It was just a funny-ass situation. In April 2021, I had a tweet where I made a joke on April Fools’. I tweeted a beat and wrote, “Drake, Trav, and Yeat, produced by me and Metro” as an April Fool’s joke. Everyone thought it was real, but it wasn’t. But then I was like, wait, this could work on the Travis and Drake song in real life. So I took the horns that I wrote, I put it on the beat, and was like this works. And the song came out literally two days later. Bro, it was crazy.

**In the past year, you’ve worked with Drake, Travis Scott, Yeat, Quavo, and many more. What would you say was your favorite project or song that you worked on?**  
I think it was working with Drake. It was really cool being with him, every day in this studio, going through ideas, building the album. I was just trying to make it the best album that it can be. And going on tour for the first time was crazy, just going to every city, seeing these different places and all these different crowds. It was inspiring. I work with a lot of different artists closely, but I never worked with an artist that closely before.

**Do you have a favorite song that you worked on?**  
My favorite song is the Drake and Yeat song \[“IDGAF”\]. Shout out to my wife, too. I was super scared to send that song because I was like, “He's not going to fuck with it.” I was trying to find a Yeat song that didn't talk about demons. So it was really hard, because at that time, every song had the word ‘demon’ in it. But we had this old song from 2021 that I love so much, and I've been trying to force him to drop it. It got to the point where I had my brother take a video of me driving to the song.

I was like, if this goes viral, he's going to drop it. It hit a mill

# Travis Scott Wants to Run the Whole Show: Inside His Paramount Deal, His Nolan Education and the Grammy That Still Hasn't Come - Variety Sweden

_The Houston rapper stepped onto a table in an Italian castle to open “The Odyssey.” Now he’s signing first-look papers at a Hollywood studio and finishing a sixth album he carries around on an iPod._

Travis Scott has played to crowds of tens of thousands. He has the highest-grossing solo rap tour in history behind him. And yet the moment he remembers most from Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” is the one where he was, by his own admission, nervous as hell.

The setup was not gentle. Scott’s first shot of the day was a close-up, delivered from the top of a wooden table inside an ancient castle on a remote Italian island, with hundreds of extras below him and Anne Hathaway, Tom Holland and Robert Pattinson watching from the room. He raised his stave and launched into the song of Odysseus: “A war. A man. A trick,” the bard’s opening account of the fall of Troy.

“All those actors were there, and I’m standing on the table,” Scott says. There was no party energy to hide behind, he adds. Camera in his face, Nolan a few feet away, everyone else locked into character.

Nolan admits the scheduling was deliberate. He put the close-up at the top of the day, threw Scott into the deep end and asked him to hold the attention of the room. He says so now with a laugh.

**Why Nolan wanted a rapper, not a musician**

The two have worked together before. Scott, then 29, contributed the end-credits track to “Tenet” in 2020, and he co-wrote “When I’m Home,” the end-credits song for “The Odyssey.” But the acting job was a separate conversation, and Nolan says he was explicit about that: he was not hiring Scott as a musician.

Adapting a nearly 2,700-year-old poem for Imax meant finding a way into the oral tradition without turning it into a museum piece. Nolan’s solution was to treat rappers as the descendants of the poets who once performed these stories aloud. He wanted someone on screen who could recite and command a room in a way a modern audience recognizes, rather than a formal, rarefied idea of a bard in the palace of Ithaca, which he says he would have found alienating.

Scott came in already knowing the text. He read “The Odyssey” as a kid in the Houston suburbs, back when he was Jacques Bermon Webster II, because his paternal grandmother Bernice Webster, an English professor, put it on his summer reading list. He also faked the essay. “I did some CliffsNotes bullshit,” he says. “I got a whoopin’ because I lied about reading it.”

His grandmother has since collected her winnings. Scott says she’s told him this is exactly why she made him read the book. Last week he posted a text from his mother, Wanda Webster, arranging to bring Grandma Bernice and his maternal grandmother, Sealie Wood, to a screening. Scott is thinking bigger: he might rent out an entire theater and fill it with family. His kids Stormi, 8, and Aire, 4, with ex Kylie Jenner, will sit this one out, given the R rating.

**A moving target**

Interviewing Scott is less a sit-down than a series of adjustments. On a Sunday afternoon in midtown Manhattan, after a photo shoot on a broiling NoMad rooftop in a Hermès suit, he keeps shifting on a low couch that his legs don’t fit, picking at the zipper of an accent pillow. He’s due uptown to catch Jay-Z at Yankee Stadium. He smokes a blunt throughout, setting it down only when a subject requires both hands.

By the time we reach his dressing room, the Rick Owens shades are off, the suit has been swapped for baggy sweatpants and a faded Oasis T-shirt layered under gold and diamond chains, and he’s deep into “The Warriors,” the 1979 gang movie he keeps returning to. He describes its characters as war heroes for peace.

That film, as it happens, is also how he and Paramount found each other.

**The Paramount deal**

Scott’s first-look deal at Paramount Pictures is being finalized as we speak, a new chapter for Cactus Jack. Paramount Pictures co-chair Josh Greenstein bonded with Scott and Cactus Jack manager and GM David Stromberg over “The Warriors” when they met to talk about expanding the brand’s footprint at the studio.

“Creativity emanates from every pore of his body,” Greenstein says, citing everything from Scott’s clothes to his cars to his taste in film. He also makes the commercial case plainly: Scott’s taste moves culture, and Greenstein counts that as a superpower.

Cactus Jack started in 2017 as a label and publishing company with artists including Sheck Wes and Don Toliver. It has since sprawled into consumer products, with collaborations spanning Nike and Jordan, “Fortnite,” Saint Laurent, Dior, Audemars Piguet, Hot Wheels, Reese’s Puffs and McDonald’s. It has already worked with Paramount on merchandise, and the limited-run “SpongeBob SquarePants” and “Scream” apparel drops sold out almost immediately.

The new agreement widens that from T-shirts to film, television, theater and experiential projects. Scott frames his interest simply: he wants to make good films, and he says Paramount isn’t afraid of good ideas.

Part of the logic is financial. His music video budgets had crept into indie-film territory, and he started asking why that money couldn’t produce something with a longer life than three or four minutes.

The studio, meanwhile, wants younger audiences back in theaters, and few artists command a fandom like Scott’s. The “Circus Maximus Tour” ran two and a half years, sold 2.2 million tickets and grossed $265 million. Paramount previewed the relationship at CinemaCon this year in a Tom Cruise-narrated reel: as Cruise pledges fresh perspectives, the camera rolls to reveal Scott, iced out, security posted in front of four chocolate-brown luxury cars in Cactus Jack’s signature shade, before he climbs onto a matching golf cart with an assistant hauling pink Goyard luggage across the lot.

**What he’d actually make**

There’s no slate yet, but he has a genre in mind. Horror, he argues, has mutated into something more interesting than horror. He’s drawn to slow dark thrillers where almost nothing happens until the end, carried by suspense, writing and a cast you don’t recognize. The Japanese film “Exit 8” is the reference point. The last thing he saw in a cinema was “Michael.”

Would he greenlight a movie about himself? Yes, though his answer is a joke and a real answer at once: “I would do ‘Entourage’ again.”

He knows Lin-Manuel Miranda is taking “The Warriors” to Broadway next spring, which hasn’t put him off doing his own version. He just hasn’t decided whether it’s a show or a film.

He is unambiguous about theaters. Streaming is fine, he says, but going out to see something with other people is the point, and he grows genuinely irritated at the idea of sound designers pouring months into a mix that ends up playing through a living-room TV speaker. He apologizes, a little sheepishly, for the rant, then relights his blunt.

**Learning the job at 5 a.m.**

Scott used the “Odyssey” shoot as an apprenticeship. He arrived at 5 a.m. and stayed until 3 p.m. whether or not he was needed, mostly to watch Nolan and cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema work. Nobody on that set retreated to a trailer, he says, which was new to him and suited him fine. He trailed the two of them asking questions and leaning into the monitor as they framed shots on Imax cameras.

The lesson he took away: see the vision through, never come up short on it. He notes that his mentor Ye told him something similar years earlier.

“The Odyssey” isn’t his first acting credit. He appeared in the 2021 indie drama “Gully” and in Harmony Korine’s “Aggro Dr1ft,” plus a cameo on HBO’s “Ballers.” He also turns up as himself in the Owen Wilson comedy “Rolling Loud,” shot at the 2024 festival, in which Wilson plays a father who sneaks his underage son into the event and ends up onstage during “Fe!n.”

He says he’d like to act more and respects people who do it as a craft. But acting means serving someone else’s vision, and Scott’s instincts run the other way. Producing, directing, composing and sound design are where he thinks he’s most useful.

Nolan sees the same thing, pointing to “Circus Maximus,” the film companion to 2023’s “Utopia,” which included segments from Nicolas Winding Refn, Korine, Gaspar Noé, Valdimar Jóhannsson, Kahlil Joseph and Scott himself. Nolan credits him with an instinctive grasp of how to pull an audience in through both ears and eyes.

Scott’s own explanation for his track record is less technical. He builds the experiences he wanted as a fan and never got.

Not everything has landed. For 2015’s “Rodeo,” his first full-length, he wanted to ship an action figure with the physical record. The idea collapsed, though he eventually got his toys anyway through McDonald’s and “Fortnite.” Far more serious was the night in 2021 when 10 people died in a crowd crush during his Astroworld Festival set in Houston, a tragedy he has described as personally devastating and which his commercial partnerships survived.

This fall, USC launches a course examining Cactus Jack as a case study in scaling personal creativity into a platform. All 140 seats went in roughly 20 minutes. “I think he understands that what drives contemporary culture is experience and immersion,” says Dr. Josh Kun of USC’s Communication and American Studies department, describing a model in which lifestyle becomes an entire way of moving through the world.

**Album six, and the trophy shelf**

The follow-up to “Utopia,” his double-platinum first No. 1, is in progress. He carries the tracks on an iPod, which fans clocked on his waistband at a recent World Cup match in Houston, where he sat with Stormi and Aire.

He won’t describe the sound, but he’ll name what’s in his ears: Parliament, Oasis, Van Halen for the mega-choruses and heavy bass lines, Don Toliver, Raphael Saadiq and Daft Punk. Touring changed his approach. He’s now writing for the person at the very back of the bowl and trying to push the live show toward something closer to theater. “Utopia” was originally conceived as a play, he notes, and he’d like to bring real-world experiences back before everything gets digitized.

With “The Odyssey” positioned as a major Oscar contender, the credits song could put him in the best original song race. Scott has been nominated for 10 Grammys and won none. “I still need a Grammy, but I would love to take home an Oscar,” he says.

Asked whether the Grammy drought drives him, he takes a long pull and thinks about it. It isn’t why he does the work, he says, but he sets goals and likes to hit them. He’s noticed that the people holding the trophies are always the ones insisting it doesn’t matter. To him, it does.

**How the song got made**

In March, Scott joined Nolan and composer Ludwig Göransson at the DGA theater in West Hollywood for a screening. Göransson had been sketching an end-credits idea with English singer-songwriter James Blake and wanted Scott involved. (One of Nolan’s favorite “Utopia” tracks is “Til Further Notice,” which features Blake.)

First Scott had to watch the film. “Travis was sitting right next to me, and during the Cyclops scene, he put his hoodie up over his head,” Göransson says, laughing. He describes Scott as a chameleon who slips out of every genre and manages to sound like the past and the future simultaneously.

A studio session was already booked for immediately after the screening. Göransson played what he had, with the bard’s lines from the nearly three-hour film sitting in the mix as placeholders, and Scott started freestyling in the gaps. He describes putting his artist hat back on to convey the whole ordeal: the trials, the attempt to get home, Penelope waiting, the years lost with Calypso. The video was shot in a castle in Switzerland.

Mid-story, Scott gets up to grab a red Airhead from the catering table. When he sits back down, he learns a piece of trivia about the song: it’s Nolan’s first songwriting credit.

“Welcome to my world, OG,” he says.

He’s due uptown to catch Jay-Z at Yankee Stadium. He smokes a blunt throughout, setting it down only when a subject requires both hands.

By the time we reach his dressing room, the Rick Owens shades are off, the suit has been swapped for baggy sweatpants and a faded Oasis T-shirt layered under gold and diamond chains, and he’s deep into “The Warriors,” the 1979 gang movie he keeps returning to. He describes its characters as war heroes for peace.

That film, as it happens, is also how he and Paramount found each other.

**The Paramount deal**

Scott’s first-look deal at Paramount Pictures is being finalized as we speak, a new chapter for Cactus Jack. Paramount Pictures co-chair Josh Greenstein bonded with Scott and Cactus Jack manager and GM David Stromberg over “The Warriors” when they met to talk about expanding the brand’s footprint at the studio.

“Creativity emanates from every pore of his body,” Greenstein says, citing everything from Scott’s clothes to his cars to his taste in film. He also makes the commercial case plainly: Scott’s taste moves culture, and Greenstein counts that as a superpower.

Cactus Jack started in 2017 as a label and publishing company with artists including Sheck Wes and Don Toliver. It has since sprawled into consumer products, with collaborations spanning Nike and Jordan, “Fortnite,” Saint Laurent, Dior, Audemars Piguet, Hot Wheels, Reese’s Puffs and McDonald’s. It has already worked with Paramount on merchandise, and the limited-run “SpongeBob SquarePants” and “Scream” apparel drops sold out almost immediately.

The new agreement widens that from T-shirts to film, television, theater and experiential projects. Scott frames his interest simply: he wants to make good films, and he says Paramount isn’t afraid of good ideas.

Part of the logic is financial. His music video budgets had crept into indie-film territory, and he started asking why that money couldn’t produce something with a longer life than three or four minutes.

The studio, meanwhile, wants younger audiences back in theaters, and few artists command a fandom like Scott’s. The “Circus Maximus Tour” ran two and a half years, sold 2.2 million tickets and grossed $265 million. Paramount previewed the relationship at CinemaCon this year in a Tom Cruise-narrated reel: as Cruise pledges fresh perspectives, the camera rolls to reveal Scott, iced out, security posted in front of four chocolate-brown luxury cars in Cactus Jack’s signature shade, before he climbs onto a matching golf cart with an assistant hauling pink Goyard luggage across the lot.

**What he’d actually make**

There’s no slate yet, but he has a genre in mind. Horror, he argues, has mutated into something more interesting than horror. He’s drawn to slow dark thrillers where almost nothing happens until the end, carried by suspense, writing and a cast you don’t recognize. The Japanese film “Exit 8” is the reference point. The last thing he saw in a cinema was “Michael.”

Would he greenlight a movie about himself? Yes, though his answer is a joke and a real answer at once: “I would do ‘Entourage’ again.”

He knows Lin-Manuel Miranda is taking “The Warriors” to Broadway next spring, which hasn’t put him off doing his own version. He just hasn’t decided whether it’s a show or a film.

He is unambiguous about theaters. Streaming is fine, he says, but going out to see something with other people is the point, and he grows genuinely irritated at the idea of sound designers pouring months into a mix that ends up playing through a living-room TV speaker. He apologizes, a little sheepishly, for the rant, then relights his blunt.

**Learning the job at 5 a.m.**

Scott used the “Odyssey” shoot as an apprenticeship. He arrived at 5 a.m. and stayed until 3 p.m. whether or not he was needed, mostly to watch Nolan and cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema work. Nobody on that set retreated to a trailer, he says, which was new to him and suited him fine. He trailed the two of them asking questions and leaning into the monitor as they framed shots on Imax cameras.

The lesson he took away: see the vision through, never come up short on it. He notes that his mentor Ye told him something similar years earlier.

“The Odyssey” isn’t his first acting credit. He appeared in the 2021 indie drama “Gully” and in Harmony Korine’s “Aggro Dr1ft,” plus a cameo on HBO’s “Ballers.” He also turns up as himself in the Owen Wilson comedy “Rolling Loud,” shot at the 2024 festival, in which Wilson plays a father who sneaks his underage son into the event and ends up onstage during “Fe!n.”

He says he’d like to act more and respects people who do it as a craft. But acting means serving someone else’s vision, and Scott’s instincts run the other way. Producing, directing, composing and sound design are where he thinks he’s most useful.

Nolan sees the same thing, pointing to “Circus Maximus,” the film companion to 2023’s “Utopia,” which included segments from Nicolas Winding Refn, Korine, Gaspar Noé, Valdimar Jóhannsson, Kahlil Joseph and Scott himself. Nolan credits him with an instinctive grasp of how to pull an audience in through both ears and eyes.

Scott’s own explanation for his track record is less technical. He builds the experiences he wanted as a fan and never got.

Not everything has landed. For 2015’s “Rodeo,” his first full-length, he wanted to ship an action figure with the physical record. The idea collapsed, though he eventually got his toys anyway through McDonald’s and “Fortnite.” Far more serious was the night in 2021 when 10 people died in a crowd crush during his Astroworld Festival set in Houston, a tragedy he has described as personally devastating and which his commercial partnerships survived.

This fall, USC launches a course examining Cactus Jack as a case study in scaling personal creativity into a platform. All 140 seats went in roughly 20 minutes. “I think he understands that what drives contemporary culture is experience and immersion,” says Dr. Josh Kun of USC’s Communication and American Studies department, describing a model in which lifestyle becomes an entire way of moving through the world.

**Album six, and the trophy shelf**

The follow-up to “Utopia,” his double-platinum first No. 1, is in progress. He carries the tracks on an iPod, which fans clocked on his waistband at a recent World Cup match in Houston, where he sat with Stormi and Aire.

He won’t describe the sound, but he’ll name what’s in his ears: Parliament, Oasis, Van Halen for the mega-choruses and heavy bass lines, Don Toliver, Raphael Saadiq and Daft Punk. Touring changed his approach. He’s now writing for the person at the very back of the bowl and trying to push the live show toward something closer to theater. “Utopia” was originally conceived as a play, he notes, and he’d like to bring real-world experiences back before everything gets digitized.

With “The Odyssey” positioned as a major Oscar contender, the credits song could put him in the best original song race. Scott has been nominated for 10 Grammys and won none. “I still need a Grammy, but I would love to take home an Oscar,” he says.

Asked whether the Grammy drought drives him, he takes a long pull and thinks about it. It isn’t why he does the work, he says, but he sets goals and likes to hit them. He’s noticed that the people holding the trophies are always the ones insisting it doesn’t matter. To him, it does.

**How the song got made**

In March, Scott joined Nolan and composer Ludwig Göransson at the DGA theater in West Hollywood for a screening. Göransson had been sketching an end-credits idea with English singer-songwriter James Blake and wanted Scott involved. (One of Nolan’s favorite “Utopia” tracks is “Til Further Notice,” which features Blake.)

First Scott had to watch the film. “Travis was sitting right next to me, and during the Cyclops scene, he put his hoodie up over his head,” Göransson says, laughing. He describes Scott as a chameleon who slips out of every genre and manages to sound like the past and the future simultaneously.

A studio session was already booked for immediately after the screening. Göransson played what he had, with the bard’s lines from the nearly three-hour film sitting in the mix as placeholders, and Scott started freestyling in the gaps. He describes putting his artist hat back on to convey the whole ordeal: the trials, the attempt to get home, Penelope waiting, the years lost with Calypso. The video was shot in a castle in Switzerland.

Mid-story, Scott gets up to grab a red Airhead from the catering table. When he sits back down, he learns a piece of trivia about the song: it’s Nolan’s first songwriting credit.

“Welcome to my world, OG,” he says.

# Travis Scott Breaks Down the Meaning of Upcoming ‘Utopia’ Album: ‘You Create It Yourself’

5/24/2023

"I'm trying to show people experiences where utopian things can exist," the rapper said.

![Travis Scott](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/02-Travis-Scott-cr-THIBAUT-GREVET-billboard-1548.jpg?w=942&h=628&crop=1)

Travis Scott THIBAUT GREVET

This month, [Travis Scott](https://www.billboard.com/artist/travis-scott/) hasn’t relented in his quest to roll out his highly anticipated album _Utopia_. After [previewing](https://www.billboard.com/music/rb-hip-hop/travis-scott-preview-utopia-album-houston-astros-locker-room-1235330291/) the project for the Houston Astros and then having his bodyguard spotted with a _Utopia_\-branded suitcase [handcuffed](https://www.billboard.com/music/rb-hip-hop/travis-scotts-utopia-bodyguard-briefcase-handcuffed-1235332581/) to his wrist last week, Scott has elected to take a new, calmer approach by covering the latest issue of _[PINUP Magazine](https://www.pinupmagazine.org/travis-scott)_.

The wildly creative cover finds the _Astroworld_ artist reimagining the alphabet through his eyes. Scott offered each letter a word and its importance when talking to the architecture and design publication. For the letter “U,” of course, Scott chose “utopia” and gave his breakdown, saying, “_Utopia_ is something that people feel is so far-fetched and out of reach, some perfect state of mind. But you create it yourself. There are people who achieve _Utopia_ every day. They may not be the richest people with the dopest cribs, but it’s a utopia wherever they are, and that’s the most you can have. With every album I live in these worlds in my mind — I’m trying to show people experiences where utopian things can exist, and you can enjoy yourself and have a good time. They can create energy that spews out magical things — new cures, new buildings, new avenues for people to move forward. People need to see that _Utopia_ is real.”

For “M,” Scott chose MPC, reveling that he “made most of my new album on an MPC.” “I got new ones; I got some old ones. My favorite is the _2000XL_. It produces a very distinctive sound that makes it feel alive,” he added.

Though _Utopia_ doesn’t have a release date, Scott’s longtime collaborator Mike Dean [said](https://www.instagram.com/p/CsnM_-OrwnP/?utm_source=ig_embed&ig_rid=1b37fc0a-222f-410b-a08b-12acfd18c122) on social media this week that he and the Houston staple are still busily chipping away on the project. “_Utopia_ will be done when Trav and I say it’s done. Do not rush. Let us cook.”

During his Fortnite takeover, Scott unleashed “The Scotts,” a sinister banger he made with Kid Cudi that debuted at No. 1. He hits play on one of the tracks. Scott is doing a two-step in front of the soundboard before the beat morphs from a bouncy summer groove to a menacing riot that sends him thrashing about. He's back in Rage Mode, his eyes tightly shut as he floats around in the utopia of his mind.

text: # Here are the full credits for Travis Scott’s UTOPIA Press Enter to Search * [Music](/music) * [Style](/style) * [Culture](/culture) * [Video](/fader-tv) * [Magazine](/magazine) * [Events](/events) * [Shop](https://shop.thefader.com/) * [US Edition](http://www.thefader.com/home) * [UK Edition](http://www.thefader.com/uk) * [Canada Edition](http://www.thefader.com/ca) July 28, 2023 ![Here are the full credits for Travis Scott’s UTOPIA](https://thefader-res.cloudinary.com/private_images/w_760,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:best/1000x1000bb-1690518223_w2nwvg/travis-scott-i-utopia-i-album-artwork.jpg) Travis Scott, _UTOPIA_ album artwork   [Travis Scott](https://www.thefader.com/artist/travis-scott-1)'s _UTOPIA_ arrived on Friday and it's a summer blockbuster to rival anything _Barbie_ or _Oppenheimer_ could offer up. Scott's first album since 2018's _Astroworld_ runs for over an hour and includes 19 tracks. The album is packed with a vast array of guests including, notably, [Beyoncé](https://www.thefader.com/artist/beyonce-1). She appears on "DELRESTO (ECHOES)," which marks her first time working with the Cactus Jack label head. That's just the tip of the guestlist, however, with [The Weeknd](https://www.thefader.com/artist/the-weeknd), [SZA](https://www.thefader.com/artist/sza), [Drake](https://www.thefader.com/artist/drake), [Bon Iver](https://www.thefader.com/artist/bon-iver), [Sampha](https://www.thefader.com/artist/sampha), [Bad Bunny](https://www.thefader.com/artist/bad-bunny), [Future](https://www.thefader.com/artist/future), and [Yung Lean](https://www.thefader.com/artist/yung-lean) also popping up at various stages. Comedian Dave Chappelle is also on the list, cropping up on "PARASAIL" Production-wise, Scott handles much of the beats but there are also credits for his regular collaborator Mike Dean, plus Kanye West, Metro Boomin, [James Blake](https://www.thefader.com/artist/james-blake), Vegyn, Tay Keith, Boi-1da, and more. [Daft Punk](https://www.thefader.com/artist/daft-punk)’s Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo is a co-producer on "MODERN JAM." It seems some credited writers were more aware of their appearances than others, with PC Music affiliate umru [tweeting his surprise](https://twitter.com/umru_/status/1684783798305574912) at seeing his name mentioned (he later [clarified](https://twitter.com/umru_/status/1684788325603753984) that "DELRESTO (ECHOES)" uses a piano sample he placed on Splice. Scott has been teasing the arrival of his new album _Utopia_ for many months now. Last week he shared the lead single ["K-POP,"](https://www.thefader.com/2023/07/21/travis-scott-bad-bunny-the-weeknd-kpop) which features [The Weeknd](https://www.thefader.com/artist/the-weeknd) and [Bad Bunny](https://www.thefader.com/artist/bad-bunny). The rapper and Cactus Jack label head had stated that he would perform in front of the Pyramids of Giza in Egypt for a [live stream event](https://www.thefader.com/2023/07/10/travis-scott-pyramids-livestream) today, July 28, to celebrate the release of the album. However, the live show was [axed](https://www.thefader.com/2023/07/26/travis-scotts-utopia-pyramids-show-canceled) shortly after Egypt’s Musicians’ Syndicate stated that they would revoke any license needed to perform due, in part, to Scott's unspecified “rituals." You can read more about the whole thing went down [here](https://www.thefader.com/2023/07/26/musicians-syndicate-travis-scott-pyramids-show). Scott also released a movie, [titled _Circus Maximus_](https://www.thefader.com/2023/07/25/travis-scott-utopia-circus-maximus-release-dates), in theaters on Thursday night. # Meet WondaGurl, The Quiet Hustler Behind Rap’s Loudest Beats

Press Enter to Search

*   [Music](/music)
*   [Style](/style)
*   [Culture](/culture)
*   [Video](/fader-tv)
*   [Magazine](/magazine)
*   [Events](/events)
*   [Shop](https://shop.thefader.com/)
*   [US Edition](http://www.thefader.com/home)
*   [UK Edition](http://www.thefader.com/uk)
*   [Canada Edition](http://www.thefader.com/ca)

![Meet WondaGurl, The Quiet Hustler Behind Rap’s Loudest Beats](https://thefader-res.cloudinary.com/private_images/w_1440,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:best/F103_genf_wonda_McIsaac_01_WEB_zgg5ne/wondagurl-producer-ebony-oshunrinde-interview.jpg)

_The FADER's longstanding series [GEN F](http://www.thefader.com/tag/gen-f) profiles emerging artists to know now.  
_

Within hip-hop’s increasingly complex constellation of celebrity, producers are now almost as beloved as rappers. At home, we feverishly catalog their beats; online, we make them into memes; in the club, we scream their drops. If a producer doesn’t have a drop in 2016, do they even exist? In the case of Ebony Oshunrinde, the young producer better known as [WondaGurl](https://soundcloud.com/wondagurl), the answer is very much yes.

I first met Oshunrinde four years ago, at a listening party in Toronto thrown by the rapper [Rich Kidd](http://richkiddbeats.com/). Though she was clearly more comfortable standing off to the side, Rich made sure everyone there knew who was responsible for the calamitous drums on [“Money Money,”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pizWZeg3rl4) his single with Vancouver rapper [SonReal](http://iamsonreal.com/). A few months later, two weeks before her 16th birthday, the quiet girl in the corner bested over 30 aspiring producers in a local Battle of the Beat Makers competition. The following summer, she became a flashpoint in the news cycle surrounding [Jay Z](http://www.thefader.com/artist/jay-z)’s _Magna Carta Holy Grail_ after co-producing “Crown,” a pummeling, post-_Yeezus_\-era Sizzla flip. She wasn’t yet a high school senior.

Oshunrinde’s suburban hometown of Brampton, Ontario, is downright quaint compared to brassy Los Angeles, where the now 19-year-old is temporarily logging studio time, doing sessions with [Big Sean](http://www.thefader.com/artist/big-sean) and [Travis Scott](http://www.thefader.com/artist/travis-scott). When we catch up on the phone, she’s friendly and upbeat but clearly still uninterested in the self-promoting side of modern life as a musician. All she wants to talk about is making beats.

![Meet WondaGurl, The Quiet Hustler Behind Rap’s Loudest Beats](https://thefader-res.cloudinary.com/private_images/w_1440,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:best/F103_genf_wonda_McIsaac_02_WEB_sft4ah/wondagurl-producer-ebony-oshunrinde-interview.jpg)

What’s she done with the spoils of placing music with Jay Z, [Drake](http://www.thefader.com/artist/drake), and [Rihanna](http://www.thefader.com/artist/rihanna)? “\[I bought\] studio equipment so I could have a nice setup in my house,” she says. How has her process changed since she broke out professionally in 2013? “I got into mixing, so everything just sounds better.” What fills those few spare hours between waking up and going to the studio? “Nothing. I just make beats.” Travel has been a bright spot, she says. “I want to go to Europe more. I’ve been to Berlin — for work.”

Big-room label meetings aren’t her favorite, but they’ve been getting easier, Oshunrinde says. “I don’t like them, but I have to — you know?” Studio sessions are harder. “I’m not really good at working with people, as weird as that sounds,” she says slowly, choosing her words carefully. “It’s just more about being comfortable. I can’t work with a random person. I have a hard time doing that.” Even her friendships revolve around beats. At home in Brampton, she spends time with the producer [Eestbound](https://soundcloud.com/eestbound); together, they combined a zooted bassline and a sped-up Lee Fields riff to make Travis Scott’s [“Antidote,”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KnZ8h3MRuYg) one of the biggest-sounding rap songs of 2015.

While she’s most known for high-profile placements, Oshunrinde’s work with Toronto artists sometimes feels more significant, not least because it reveals what she’s like as a solo producer. Tracks like [Jahkoy](http://www.thefader.com/artist/Jahkoy)’s twinkling [“Odd Future”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DLgTucmif_Q) show a softer side. One of her best beats is for [“YKTO (You Know the Ones)”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qJ5PJWkll6I) by [Redway](http://www.thefader.com/artist/Redway), a beloved local rapper who was killed in a car accident in August 2015. “He was like my brother,” she says. The song’s groaning undercarriage and zig-zagging synth loops sound borderline 3D when amplified by a diligent kick and some silky hi-hats. Below Redway’s teasing cadence, the beat is polished and genuinely uplifting. “No one in Toronto was making feel-good music \[at that time\],” she says. “I like to hear things I’ve never heard before.”

![Meet WondaGurl, The Quiet Hustler Behind Rap’s Loudest Beats](https://thefader-res.cloudinary.com/private_images/w_1440,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:best/F103_genf_wonda_McIsaac_03_WEB_djg5zh/wondagurl-producer-ebony-oshunrinde-interview.jpg)

It’s thanks to Oshunrinde’s head-down focus and chameleonic production style — sometimes industrial, sometimes psychedelic — that she has outlasted those first 15 minutes of fame. Though she’s the rare woman making rap beats full-time, she notably lacks a gender parity agenda. Consistently she’s been less focused on the industry’s problems and more concerned with setting a positive example through hard work. “I dream about completely taking over the game, in a Timbaland kind of way,” she tells me. WondaGurl’s beats might not have a drop, but she definitely wants recognition. From what she’s accomplished already, she deserves plenty.

# Goosebumps by Travis Scott (featuring Kendrick Lamar) - Songfacts

![Play Video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/Dst9gZkq1a8/hqdefault.jpg)

#### Songfacts®:

*   This love song finds Travis Scott so in love with his girl, he gets goosebumps. Goosebumps are a condition of the skin, like that of a plucked goose. The bristling feeling a person feels is due to the raising of hairs when they are cold or experience strong emotions such as fear, euphoria or sexual arousal.
    
*   This song features a verse by Kendrick Lamar. Travi$ Scott debuted his entire new album, **Birds in the Trap Sing McKnigh**t, during an episode of his .Wav radio show on Beats 1. "It's crazy how we got these legends on the album," Scott told his .Wav listeners. "It's so dope how they came to Trav world and turned up. Kendrick turned up... This is the illest rapper in the f--king game."
    
*   Scott first met Kendrick Lamar at the MTV Video Music Awards. He recalled to _Billboard_ magazine: "He came up to me and was just like, 'Yo, man, I f--k with your music. It's super dope and inspirational'" I was like, whoa, this is the best rapper in the globe - he f--ks with my music! That's one of the things that made me want to keep working on my music and try to keep it going 'cause I'm not the most rappity rap ass n---a. That's not me but I really love Kendrick's music."
    
*   The song was recorded at Scott's home in Beverly Hills with production by regular Lamar beatmakers Cardo and Yung Exclusive plus German production duo Cubeatz.
    
*   It was Cardo who came up with the original beat. According to the producer, several rappers had access to the instrumentation before Scott. He tweeted:
    
    "U know how many niggas had the 'goosebumps' beat before Travis and they didn't do nothing to it ? U wouldn't believe it."
    
    Speaking with [DJBooth](http://www.djbooth.net), Cardo named the names that passed on his instrumentation. "Only three to four people had that beat," he said. "That was Drake, ScHoolboy Q, Future—don't know if he ever got it—Rihanna and I sent it to Young Thug as well."
    
*   During a May 12, 2017 gig at The Criterion in Oklahoma City, Travis Scott rapped this song 14 times in a row. Scott claimed this was a world record for most times a tune has been performed by an artist in a single concert, usurping Jay Z and Kanye West who back in 2012 during their _Watch the Throne Tour_, performed "[Niggas in Paris](https://www.songfacts.com/facts/the-throne/niggas-in-paris)" 12 times in a row. However, a quick search of the Guinness World Records database suggests that neither Jay-Z/West nor Scott's performances are officially recognized as record breakers.
    
    Apparently, that feat wasn't good enough for Scott, so he decided to break his own personal record by performing the song fifteen times in a row during his _Birds Eye View_ tour stop in Cleveland on May 21, 2017. Scott couldn't wait to tweet the news. "GOOSEBUMPS GOT PERFORM 15 TIMES. I LEFT MY CLOTHES FOR ROCK AND ROLL HALL OF FAME," he wrote. However, the rapper actually only performed the song's hook over and over again - so we're not sure if that counts?
    
*   Scott recruited the Brooklyn-based directing duo BRTHR, who consist of Alex Lee and Kyle Wightman for the song's music video. The pair told [Genius](https://genius.com/Travis-scott-goosebumps-lyrics/) that they wanted to create something that teenagers would remember. "The video is basically about this hellish freak show and Travis' kind of journey to hell" Wightman said.
    
    Lee added, "We wanted to have the video kind of hit hard right from the beginning and just draw people in."
    
*   BRTHR based the clip on their video for The Weeknd's "[Party Monster](https://www.songfacts.com/facts/the-weeknd/party-monster)." Scott told them in a meeting that he wanted a similar aesthetic, but with the addition of strippers.
    
    "Our goal wasn't to make this super, super dark video anyways," Lee said. "It was a mixture. It was dark and lighthearted. It's like, let's lighten the mood up with 3D girls in bikinis in hell."
    
*   The song featured in the 2018 movie drama _The Hate U Give_.
    
*   The Spanish DJ and producer HVME (an abbreviation of his civil name, pronounced "Hume") [reworked the song](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W5b-a8Nzmag) in mid-2020. The Spaniard transformed Scott's trap-hop original into a sleek, deep-house banger. Released on June 11, 2020, it soon began clocking up streams and entering charts around the world.
    
    On January 15, 2021 HVME teamed up with Scott for the official remix.
    
*   "Goosebumps" soundtracks the trailer for the Disney+ 2023 series of the same title. The trailer for _Goosebumps_ features several jump scares and bone-chilling scenes synched by the eerie and atmospheric track.

# Is Travis Scott’s Own Rapping the Weak Point on ‘Utopia’?

Music Now

Travis Scott's new album, _Utopia_, has innovative production and guests from Beyoncé to Future to SZA — but critics are singling out its creator as a hollow presence at its center

[Travis Scott](https://www.rollingstone.com/t/travis-scott/)‘s _[Utopia](https://www.rollingstone.com/t/utopia/)_ has only been out for two and a half weeks, but it’s already spawned numerous strands of discourse, from the apparent [debt](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/utopia-kanye-similarities-1234801053/) its production owes to various scrapped Kanye West songs to the debate over whether its lyrics should have more extensively addressed Scott’s reaction to the fatal crowd crush at his [2021 Astroworld Festival](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/eyewitnesses-astroworld-houston-travis-scott-1254208/).

The discography of [Travis Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travis_Scott "Travis Scott"), an American rapper and record producer, consists of four [studio albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_album "Studio album"), two collaborative [extended plays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_play "Extended play") (EPs), two [compilation albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compilation_albums "Compilation albums"), 83 [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_\(music\) "Single (music)") (including 35 as a featured artist), five [mixtapes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixtape "Mixtape"), (including three collaborative mixtapes), seven [promotional singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promotional_recording "Promotional recording"), 43 [music videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video "Music video"), and one [collaborative album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaborative_album "Collaborative album"). Following two mixtape releases—_[Owl Pharaoh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owl_Pharaoh "Owl Pharaoh")_ and _[Days Before Rodeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Days_Before_Rodeo "Days Before Rodeo")_ (which has been re-released to [streaming media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media") as a celebration of its tenth anniversary on August 23, 2024, and reached the top spot of the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"))—between 2013 and 2014 respectively, his debut studio album, _[Rodeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodeo_\(Travis_Scott_album\) "Rodeo (Travis Scott album)")_ (2015), reached at number 3 on the _Billboard_ 200 and produced the top-20 single—"[Antidote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antidote_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Antidote (Travis Scott song)")"—that has reached at number 16 on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"). His second studio album, _[Birds in the Trap Sing McKnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birds_in_the_Trap_Sing_McKnight "Birds in the Trap Sing McKnight")_ (2016), debuted atop the _Billboard_ 200 and gave Scott his first chart-topping project, and also produced the top-40 single—"[Goosebumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goosebumps_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Goosebumps (Travis Scott song)")" (featuring [Kendrick Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendrick_Lamar "Kendrick Lamar"))—that has reached at number 32 on the _Billboard_ Hot 100. His first collaborative album, _[Huncho Jack, Jack Huncho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huncho_Jack,_Jack_Huncho "Huncho Jack, Jack Huncho")_ (2017; with [Quavo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quavo "Quavo")), under the name [Huncho Jack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huncho_Jack "Huncho Jack"), which is a name after Quavo's nickname of "Huncho" and Scott's nickname of "Jack". In 2018, Scott released the single, "[Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watch_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Watch (Travis Scott song)")" (featuring [Lil Uzi Vert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Uzi_Vert "Lil Uzi Vert") and [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West "Kanye West")), which charted at number 16 on the Hot 100.

His third studio album, _[Astroworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astroworld_\(album\) "Astroworld (album)")_ (2018), debuted atop the _Billboard_ 200 and giving Scott his second chart-topping project, and also produced the _Billboard_ Hot 100 number-one single—"[Sicko Mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicko_Mode "Sicko Mode")"—that gave Scott his first number-one single and produced the top-40 single—"[Yosemite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yosemite_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Yosemite (Travis Scott song)")"—that has reached at number 25 on the Hot 100. "[Wake Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_Up_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Wake Up (Travis Scott song)")" was released as a single in 2019, becoming a top-40 single, and reached at number 30 on the Hot 100. The promotional single, "[Stargazing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stargazing_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Stargazing (Travis Scott song)")", also reached number 8 on the Hot 100. Also in 2019, [Ed Sheeran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Sheeran "Ed Sheeran") collaborated with Scott on a song, "[Antisocial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisocial_\(Ed_Sheeran_and_Travis_Scott_song\) "Antisocial (Ed Sheeran and Travis Scott song)")", which charted at number 37 on the Hot 100. Later that same year, he released the single, "[Highest in the Room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highest_in_the_Room "Highest in the Room")", which became his second number-one single. His first compilation album with his record label, [Cactus Jack Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cactus_Jack_Records "Cactus Jack Records") (named as JackBoys), _[JackBoys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JackBoys "JackBoys")_ (2019), debuted atop the _Billboard_ 200 and gave Scott his third chart-topping project, but was not credited for the song. The album produced the top-40 single, "[Out West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_West_\(song\) "Out West (song)")" (featuring [Young Thug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Thug "Young Thug")), which reached at number 38 on the Hot 100. In 2020, he collaborated with [Kid Cudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_Cudi "Kid Cudi") on a song—"[The Scotts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Scotts "The Scotts")" (under the name the Scotts)—which became his third number-one single and released the single—"[Franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franchise_\(song\) "Franchise (song)")" (featuring Young Thug and [M.I.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M.I.A._\(rapper\) "M.I.A. (rapper)"))—that became his fourth number-one single. In 2021, Scott collaborated with [Lil Baby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Baby "Lil Baby") and [Lil Durk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Durk "Lil Durk") on a song, "Hats Off" (debuted at number 16 on the Hot 100), and collaborated with Thug and [Drake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drake_\(musician\) "Drake (musician)") on "[Bubbly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubbly_\(Young_Thug,_Drake_and_Travis_Scott_song\) "Bubbly (Young Thug, Drake and Travis Scott song)")", which debuted at number 20 on the Hot 100. Also that same year, he released the top-20 single—"[Escape Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escape_Plan_\(song\) "Escape Plan (song)")"—and the top-40 single—"[Mafia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mafia_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Mafia (Travis Scott song)")"—with both songs peaking at numbers 11 and 26 on the Hot 100, respectively. In 2022, two of Scott's collaborations with [Metro Boomin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Boomin "Metro Boomin") peaked in the top 40 of the Hot 100, with "[Niagara Falls (Foot or 2)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls_\(Foot_or_2\) "Niagara Falls (Foot or 2)")" (also with [21 Savage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21_Savage "21 Savage")) and "[Raindrops (Insane)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raindrops_\(Insane\) "Raindrops (Insane)")", charting at numbers 27 and 31, respectively. His fourth studio album, _[Utopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utopia_\(Travis_Scott_album\) "Utopia (Travis Scott album)")_ (2023), debuted atop the _Billboard_ 200, giving Scott his fourth chart-topping project and his third with him being credited for that record. It produced two top-5 singles—"[Meltdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meltdown_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Meltdown (Travis Scott song)")" (featuring Drake) and "[Fein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fein_\(song\) "Fein (song)")" (featuring [Playboi Carti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playboi_Carti "Playboi Carti"))—with both songs peaked numbers 3 and 5 on the _Billboard_ Hot 100, respectively, while also produced the top-10 single—"[K-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-pop_\(Travis_Scott,_Bad_Bunny_and_the_Weeknd_song\) "K-pop (Travis Scott, Bad Bunny and the Weeknd song)")" (a collaboration with [Bad Bunny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Bunny "Bad Bunny") and [the Weeknd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Weeknd "The Weeknd"))—that debuted at number 7 on the Hot 100, produced the top-20 single—"[I Know ?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Know_%3F "I Know ?")"—that debuted at number 11 on the Hot 100, and also produced the top-40 single—"[Delresto (Echoes)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delresto_\(Echoes\) "Delresto (Echoes)")" (with [Beyoncé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyoncé "Beyoncé"))—that debuted at number 25 on the Hot 100. In 2024, Scott collaborated with Savage and Metro on a song, "[Née-Nah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Née-Nah "Née-Nah")", which debuted at number 10 on the Hot 100. Later that same year, both of his collaborations with Future and Metro debuted in the top 10 of the Hot 100, with "[Type Shit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_Shit "Type Shit")" (also with Carti) and "[Cinderella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinderella_\(Future,_Metro_Boomin_and_Travis_Scott_song\) "Cinderella (Future, Metro Boomin and Travis Scott song)")", charting at numbers 2 and 6, respectively. In 2025, Scott released the single—"[4x4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4x4_\(song\) "4x4 (song)")"—that became his fifth number-one single and two of his collaborations with Carti debuted in the top 40 of the Hot 100, with "[Crush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crush_\(Playboi_Carti_and_Travis_Scott_song\) "Crush (Playboi Carti and Travis Scott song)")" and "[Philly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philly_\(Playboi_Carti_and_Travis_Scott_song\) "Philly (Playboi Carti and Travis Scott song)")" charting at numbers 20 and 28, respectively. His second compilation album with Cactus Jack (JackBoys), _[JackBoys 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JackBoys_2 "JackBoys 2")_ (2025), debuted atop the _Billboard_ 200 and gave Scott his fifth chart-topping project.

Scott has been featured on several songs that have received mainstream success, starting with his 2017's appearance on [SZA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SZA "SZA")'s single, "[Love Galore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Galore "Love Galore")", which reached number 32 on the Hot 100. Later that same year he appeared, alongside Quavo, on Drake's single, "[Portland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_\(song\) "Portland (song)")", which reached number 9 on the Hot 100. Scott then appeared on Savage, [Offset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offset_\(rapper\) "Offset (rapper)"), and Metro's song, "[Ghostface Killers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghostface_Killers "Ghostface Killers")", which charted at number 35 on the Hot 100. Later that same year, he appeared on [Miguel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_\(singer\) "Miguel (singer)")'s single, "[Sky Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Walker_\(song\) "Sky Walker (song)")", which charted at number 29 on the Hot 100. In 2018, Scott appeared, alongside Offset, on [Kodak Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodak_Black "Kodak Black")'s single, "[Zeze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeze_\(song\) "Zeze (song)")", which reached number 2 on the Hot 100, serving as his highest-charting song as a featured artist. In 2019, he appeared, alongside [J. Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Cole "J. Cole"), on Thug's single, "[The London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_London "The London")", which reached number 12 on the Hot 100. Later that same year, Scott appeared, alongside [Ozzy Osbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne "Ozzy Osbourne"), on [Post Malone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone "Post Malone")'s single, "[Take What You Want](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_What_You_Want "Take What You Want")", which charted at number 8 on the Hot 100. In 2020, he appeared on [Nav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nav_\(rapper\) "Nav (rapper)") and [Gunna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunna_\(rapper\) "Gunna (rapper)")'s single, "[Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turks_\(song\) "Turks (song)")", which peaked at number 17 on the Hot 100. Later that same year, Scott appeared on Future's song, "[Solitaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solitaires "Solitaires")", which entered at number 32 on the Hot 100. In 2021, he appeared, alongside [Baby Keem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_Keem "Baby Keem"), on West's song, "[Praise God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praise_God "Praise God")", which peaked at number 20 on the Hot 100. Later that same year, Scott appeared on Drake's song, "[Fair Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Trade_\(song\) "Fair Trade (song)")", which peaked at number 3 on the Hot 100. In 2022, he appeared on Drake and Savage's song, "[Pussy & Millions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pussy_&_Millions "Pussy & Millions")", which charted at number 6 on the Hot 100. In 2023, Scott appeared on Uzi's song, "[Aye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye_\(Lil_Uzi_Vert_song\) "Aye (Lil Uzi Vert song)")", which peaked at number 31 on the Hot 100. In 2024, he appeared, alongside Carti, on [¥$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/¥$ "¥$") (West and [Ty Dolla Sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ty_Dolla_Sign "Ty Dolla Sign"))'s song, "[Fuk Sumn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuk_Sumn "Fuk Sumn")", which entered at number 23 on the Hot 100.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/2025-0120_Cole_Gahagan_Michael_Rubin_Travis_Scott_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-2025-0120_Cole_Gahagan_Michael_Rubin_Travis_Scott_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2025-0120_Cole_Gahagan_Michael_Rubin_Travis_Scott_\(cropped\).jpg)

The discography of [Travis Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travis_Scott "Travis Scott"), an American rapper and record producer, consists of four [studio albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_album "Studio album"), two collaborative [extended plays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_play "Extended play") (EPs), two [compilation albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compilation_albums "Compilation albums"), 83 [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_\(music\) "Single (music)") (including 35 as a featured artist), five [mixtapes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixtape "Mixtape"), (including three collaborative mixtapes), seven [promotional singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promotional_recording "Promotional recording"), 43 [music videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video "Music video"), and one [collaborative album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaborative_album "Collaborative album"). Following two mixtape releases—_[Owl Pharaoh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owl_Pharaoh "Owl Pharaoh")_ and _[Days Before Rodeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Days_Before_Rodeo "Days Before Rodeo")_ (which has been re-released to [streaming media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media") as a celebration of its tenth anniversary on August 23, 2024, and reached the top spot of the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"))—between 2013 and 2014 respectively, his debut studio album, _[Rodeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodeo_\(Travis_Scott_album\) "Rodeo (Travis Scott album)")_ (2015), reached at number 3 on the _Billboard_ 200 and produced the top-20 single—"[Antidote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antidote_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Antidote (Travis Scott song)")"—that has reached at number 16 on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"). His second studio album, _[Birds in the Trap Sing McKnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birds_in_the_Trap_Sing_McKnight "Birds in the Trap Sing McKnight")_ (2016), debuted atop the _Billboard_ 200 and gave Scott his first chart-topping project, and also produced the top-40 single—"[Goosebumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goosebumps_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Goosebumps (Travis Scott song)")" (featuring [Kendrick Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendrick_Lamar "Kendrick Lamar"))—that has reached at number 32 on the _Billboard_ Hot 100. His first collaborative album, _[Huncho Jack, Jack Huncho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huncho_Jack,_Jack_Huncho "Huncho Jack, Jack Huncho")_ (2017; with [Quavo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quavo "Quavo")), under the name [Huncho Jack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huncho_Jack "Huncho Jack"), which is a name after Quavo's nickname of "Huncho" and Scott's nickname of "Jack". In 2018, Scott released the single, "[Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watch_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Watch (Travis Scott song)")" (featuring [Lil Uzi Vert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Uzi_Vert "Lil Uzi Vert") and [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West "Kanye West")), which charted at number 16 on the Hot 100.

His third studio album, _[Astroworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astroworld_\(album\) "Astroworld (album)")_ (2018), debuted atop the _Billboard_ 200 and giving Scott his second chart-topping project, and also produced the _Billboard_ Hot 100 number-one single—"[Sicko Mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicko_Mode "Sicko Mode")"—that gave Scott his first number-one single and produced the top-40 single—"[Yosemite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yosemite_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Yosemite (Travis Scott song)")"—that has reached at number 25 on the Hot 100. "[Wake Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_Up_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Wake Up (Travis Scott song)")" was released as a single in 2019, becoming a top-40 single, and reached at number 30 on the Hot 100. The promotional single, "[Stargazing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stargazing_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Stargazing (Travis Scott song)")", also reached number 8 on the Hot 100. Also in 2019, [Ed Sheeran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Sheeran "Ed Sheeran") collaborated with Scott on a song, "[Antisocial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisocial_\(Ed_Sheeran_and_Travis_Scott_song\) "Antisocial (Ed Sheeran and Travis Scott song)")", which charted at number 37 on the Hot 100. Later that same year, he released the single, "[Highest in the Room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highest_in_the_Room "Highest in the Room")", which became his second number-one single. His first compilation album with his record label, [Cactus Jack Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cactus_Jack_Records "Cactus Jack Records") (named as JackBoys), _[JackBoys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JackBoys "JackBoys")_ (2019), debuted atop the _Billboard_ 200 and gave Scott his third chart-topping project, but was not credited for the song. The album produced the top-40 single, "[Out West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_West_\(song\) "Out West (song)")" (featuring [Young Thug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Thug "Young Thug")), which reached at number 38 on the Hot 100. In 2020, he collaborated with [Kid Cudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_Cudi "Kid Cudi") on a song—"[The Scotts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Scotts "The Scotts")" (under the name the Scotts)—which became his third number-one single and released the single—"[Franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franchise_\(song\) "Franchise (song)")" (featuring Young Thug and [M.I.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M.I.A._\(rapper\) "M.I.A. (rapper)"))—that became his fourth number-one single. In 2021, Scott collaborated with [Lil Baby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Baby "Lil Baby") and [Lil Durk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Durk "Lil Durk") on a song, "Hats Off" (debuted at number 16 on the Hot 100), and collaborated with Thug and [Drake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drake_\(musician\) "Drake (musician)") on "[Bubbly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubbly_\(Young_Thug,_Drake_and_Travis_Scott_song\) "Bubbly (Young Thug, Drake and Travis Scott song)")", which debuted at number 20 on the Hot 100. Also that same year, he released the top-20 single—"[Escape Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escape_Plan_\(song\) "Escape Plan (song)")"—and the top-40 single—"[Mafia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mafia_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Mafia (Travis Scott song)")"—with both songs peaking at numbers 11 and 26 on the Hot 100, respectively. In 2022, two of Scott's collaborations with [Metro Boomin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Boomin "Metro Boomin") peaked in the top 40 of the Hot 100, with "[Niagara Falls (Foot or 2)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls_\(Foot_or_2\) "Niagara Falls (Foot or 2)")" (also with [21 Savage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21_Savage "21 Savage")) and "[Raindrops (Insane)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raindrops_\(Insane\) "Raindrops (Insane)")", charting at numbers 27 and 31, respectively. His fourth studio album, _[Utopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utopia_\(Travis_Scott_album\) "Utopia (Travis Scott album)")_ (2023), debuted atop the _Billboard_ 200, giving Scott his fourth chart-topping project and his third with him being credited for that record. It produced two top-5 singles—"[Meltdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meltdown_\(Travis_Scott_song\) "Meltdown (Travis Scott song)")" (featuring Drake) and "[Fein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fein_\(song\) "Fein (song)")" (featuring [Playboi Carti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playboi_Carti "Playboi Carti"))—with both songs peaked numbers 3 and 5 on the _Billboard_ Hot 100, respectively, while also produced the top-10 single—"[K-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-pop_\(Travis_Scott,_Bad_Bunny_and_the_Weeknd_song\) "K-pop (Travis Scott, Bad Bunny and the Weeknd song)")" (a collaboration with [Bad Bunny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Bunny "Bad Bunny") and [the Weeknd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Weeknd "The Weeknd"))—that debuted at number 7 on the Hot 100, produced the top-20 single—"[I Know ?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Know_%3F "I Know ?")"—that debuted at number 11 on the Hot 100, and also produced the top-40 single—"[Delresto (Echoes)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delresto_\(Echoes\) "Delresto (Echoes)")" (with [Beyoncé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyoncé "Beyoncé"))—that debuted at number 25 on the Hot 100. In 2024, Scott collaborated with Savage and Metro on a song, "[Née-Nah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Née-Nah "Née-Nah")", which debuted at number 10 on the Hot 100. Later that same year, both of his collaborations with Future and Metro debuted in the top 10 of the Hot 100, with "[Type Shit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_Shit "Type Shit")" (also with Carti) and "[Cinderella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinderella_\(Future,_Metro_Boomin_and_Travis_Scott_song\) "Cinderella (Future, Metro Boomin and Travis Scott song)")", charting at numbers 2 and 6, respectively. In 2025, Scott released the single—"[4x4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4x4_\(song\) "4x4 (song)")"—that became his fifth number-one single and two of his collaborations with Carti debuted in the top 40 of the Hot 100, with "[Crush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crush_\(Playboi_Carti_and_Travis_Scott_song\) "Crush (Playboi Carti and Travis Scott song)")" and "[Philly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philly_\(Playboi_Carti_and_Travis_Scott_song\) "Philly (Playboi Carti and Travis Scott song)")" charting at numbers 20 and 28, respectively. His second compilation album with Cactus Jack (JackBoys), _[JackBoys 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JackBoys_2 "JackBoys 2")_ (2025), debuted atop the _Billboard_ 200 and gave Scott his fifth chart-topping project.

Scott has been featured on several songs that have received mainstream success, starting with his 2017's appearance on [SZA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SZA "SZA")'s single, "[Love Galore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Galore "Love Galore")", which reached number 32 on the Hot 100. Later that same year he appeared, alongside Quavo, on Drake's single, "[Portland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_\(song\) "Portland (song)")", which reached number 9 on the Hot 100. Scott then appeared on Savage, [Offset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offset_\(rapper\) "Offset (rapper)"), and Metro's song, "[Ghostface Killers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghostface_Killers "Ghostface Killers")", which charted at number 35 on the Hot 100. Later that same year, he appeared on [Miguel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_\(singer\) "Miguel (singer)")'s single, "[Sky Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Walker_\(song\) "Sky Walker (song)")", which charted at number 29 on the Hot 100. In 2018, Scott appeared, alongside Offset, on [Kodak Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodak_Black "Kodak Black")'s single, "[Zeze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeze_\(song\) "Zeze (song)")", which reached number 2 on the Hot 100, serving as his highest-charting song as a featured artist. In 2019, he appeared, alongside [J. Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Cole "J. Cole"), on Thug's single, "[The London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_London "The London")", which reached number 12 on the Hot 100. Later that same year, Scott appeared, alongside [Ozzy Osbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne "Ozzy Osbourne"), on [Post Malone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone "Post Malone")'s single, "[Take What You Want](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_What_You_Want "Take What You Want")", which charted at number 8 on the Hot 100. In 2020, he appeared on [Nav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nav_\(rapper\) "Nav (rapper)") and [Gunna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunna_\(rapper\) "Gunna (rapper)")'s single, "[Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turks_\(song\) "Turks (song)")", which peaked at number 17 on the Hot 100. Later that same year, Scott appeared on Future's song, "[Solitaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solitaires "Solitaires")", which entered at number 32 on the Hot 100. In 2021, he appeared, alongside [Baby Keem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_Keem "Baby Keem"), on West's song, "[Praise God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praise_God "Praise God")", which peaked at number 20 on the Hot 100. Later that same year, Scott appeared on Drake's song, "[Fair Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Trade_\(song\) "Fair Trade (song)")", which peaked at number 3 on the Hot 100. In 2022, he appeared on Drake and Savage's song, "[Pussy & Millions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pussy_&_Millions "Pussy & Millions")", which charted at number 6 on the Hot 100. In 2023, Scott appeared on Uzi's song, "[Aye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye_\(Lil_Uzi_Vert_song\) "Aye (Lil Uzi Vert song)")", which peaked at number 31 on the Hot 100. In 2024, he appeared, alongside Carti, on [¥$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/¥$ "¥$") (West and [Ty Dolla Sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ty_Dolla_Sign "Ty Dolla Sign"))'s song, "[Fuk Sumn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuk_Sumn "Fuk Sumn")", which entered at number 23 on the Hot 100.

# Wondagurl - NYLON February 16

They say not all heroes wear capes. Case in point: 19-year-old producer WondaGurl, whose impressive impact on the male-dominated hip-hop scene just might qualify as superhuman.

Born Ebony Oshunrinde, WondaGurl spent her preteen years in Toronto channeling many creative passions through different media. “I was doing a whole bunch of things: making video games and music videos, learning how to engineer,” she says. Influenced by hitmakers Timbaland and Boi-1da (who inspired her moniker), she got her start by following YouTube videos and tinkering on her Casio keyboard. 

Toronto’s 2012 Battle of the Beatmakers marked her public debut. Not only did her talent become known when she took home the competition’s title at the ripe age of 15, but her stoic response to the victory also made apparent her inherent shyness, a quality that’s quite rare in an industry full of loud personalities. “In the second round, before I went on \[stage\] again, I was way too scared to even go,” the producer recalls, laughing. “It was one of the worst experiences, but the best at the same time.” 

WondaGurl’s beats surely compensate for whatever rambunctiousness she lacks. Each track enchants with a creeping darkness, balanced out by drums that can likely overpower any unworthy sound system. This is evident on Travis Scott’s “Uptown,” one of her favorite singles on which to have worked. “He is a very hype person, so working with him is very turnt up all the time,” WondaGurl says of Scott, her longtime friend and collaborator, who coordinated her first major project—it was he who sent Jay Z the reggae-infused beat that became “Crown” on 2013’s _Magna Carta Holy Grail_. After Hov tweeted that working with WondaGurl was, “at the risk of sounding redundant, wondarful,” nary a music site overlooked that a 16-year-old girl was involved with the hip-hop icon’s album.

"**4x4**" is a song by American rapper and singer [Travis Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travis_Scott "Travis Scott"). It was released as a single through [Cactus Jack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cactus_Jack_Records "Cactus Jack Records") and [Epic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_Records "Epic Records") on January 24, 2025. Scott wrote the song with producers [Tay Keith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tay_Keith "Tay Keith") and [FnZ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FnZ "FnZ") (Finatik and Zac), alongside Dougie F, with additional writing credits going to [Honorable C.N.O.T.E.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorable_C.N.O.T.E. "Honorable C.N.O.T.E."), as the song samples the 2016 [Tennessee State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_State_University "Tennessee State University") marching band playing an instrumental version of the song "Say Sum" by [Migos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migos "Migos"). [Mike Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Dean_\(record_producer\) "Mike Dean (record producer)") mixed and mastered it, with Tommy Rush providing assistance in mixing.[\[1\]](#cite_note-1)

The song was first played through the speakers during Scott's performance at a nightclub called the Joy Room in Mexico City on September 22, 2024.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) The song was further teased on October 18 on an episode of _[WWE SmackDown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWE_SmackDown "WWE SmackDown")_ when [WWE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWE "WWE") Superstar [Roman Reigns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Reigns "Roman Reigns") had a file of the song in advance.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) Scott performed it live for the first time during the final show of his [Circus Maximus Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circus_Maximus_Tour "Circus Maximus Tour") at [Eden Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eden_Park "Eden Park") in Auckland, New Zealand on October 30. He then performed a shortened version of it during his headlining performance at the [Rolling Loud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Loud "Rolling Loud") music festival on December 14. On January 6, 2025, Scott appeared in-person at _[WWE Raw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWE_Raw "WWE Raw")'s_ [premiere on Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWE_Raw_premiere_on_Netflix "WWE Raw premiere on Netflix"), in which the song's title was revealed and it was confirmed to serve as the program's opening theme.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) He performed the song at the [2025 College Football Playoff National Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_College_Football_Playoff_National_Championship "2025 College Football Playoff National Championship") during the halftime show on January 20.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) On the same day, he shared a link to pre-save the song and restocked new merchandise on his website, in which all the proceeds would support people who were affected by the [2025 California wildfires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_California_wildfires "2025 California wildfires").[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)

A music video was released on January 24, 2025. It was directed by [Gabriel Moses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Moses?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gabriel Moses (page does not exist)") and filmed in Scott's hometown of [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston"), [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas").[\[7\]](#cite_note-7)

Critics have described the video as chaotic, high-energy, and possessing a surreal, fever-dream-like quality.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) It features imagery related to Texas (such as the [state flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texan_flag "Texan flag"), [cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowboy "Cowboy"), military personnel, and marching bands) consistent with Scott's "Cactus Jack" cowboy aesthetics, alongside wrestling and superhero themes. The visuals make use of black-and-white colors and vintage film effects.

The video opens with an altered version of the [Columbia Pictures logo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torch_Lady "Torch Lady") in which the Torch Lady flips off the camera.

"4x4" was released by [Cactus Jack]
